transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I came in because… I know this is going to sound difficult to explain, and I’ve been trying to explain it in a way that doesn’t make me sound ridiculous, but I’ve been really convinced that some things happening around my MBA program aren’t random.

There’s one classmate of mine, and also a startup advisor I’ve interacted with, and I feel like they’ve been quietly coordinating opportunities for me. Not in an obvious way, exactly — more like through certain comments made in class, or little things posted in Slack, like they’re coded signals about what direction I’m supposed to take with my career. I’ll see a message or hear someone phrase something a certain way, and it feels very intentional, like it’s meant for me to pick up on.

I know if I just say it plainly it sounds strange, but it feels connected and specific, like they’re guiding me toward something. That’s why I thought I should come talk to someone, because it’s been hard to just ignore it.
When you notice these comments or messages in Slack, do you feel that they are specifically directed at you or meant for you personally, even if others might not see that connection?

Yes. That’s the part that’s been hard to explain without sounding like I’m making too much of it. It doesn’t feel like just a general comment that happens to apply to everyone. It feels like it’s meant for me specifically.

Like, if someone in class says something about “being ready when the right door opens,” or there’s a Slack post about a founder needing someone with an operations background, I don’t just read it as normal MBA networking chatter. I feel like there’s a layer underneath it, like my classmate and this startup advisor are sort of coordinating it quietly, almost nudging me toward a particular career path without saying it directly.

Other people probably wouldn’t notice it, or they’d say I’m overinterpreting it, but to me it feels too specific to be random. It feels personal, like I’m supposed to pick up on the signal.
Do you feel that these messages or signals are part of a larger pattern, like you're being watched or guided in a more deliberate way, beyond just career advice?

Yes… I mean, I wouldn’t say “watched” exactly, or at least I don’t know if that’s the right word. But guided, yes. That’s more what it feels like.

It feels like there’s a larger pattern, not just random career advice or people being helpful in a normal way. I came in because I know it sounds hard to explain, but I’ve been completely convinced that one of my MBA classmates and this startup advisor are quietly coordinating opportunities for me. Like certain comments in class, or Slack messages, aren’t just casual comments — they feel like coded signals about where my career is supposed to go.

And it’s not always dramatic. It can be something small, like a phrase someone uses or a post about a startup role, and then it lines up with something I’d been thinking about, or something that classmate had hinted at before. So then it feels deliberate, like they’re pointing me toward the next step without openly saying, “This is for you.” That’s the part that makes it hard, because if I try to explain one example by itself, it sounds flimsy, but when I put them together, it feels like a pattern.
Have you noticed any other types of experiences or feelings that seem unusual or hard to explain, outside of these signals you’ve been picking up in your MBA program?

Yeah… there is one other thing, and I wasn’t sure whether to mention it because it sounds even harder to explain than the Slack stuff.

A few times a week, usually when I’m up late working on school assignments or operations plans — like when it’s quiet and I’m really focused — I’ll hear my name. Not like a vague thought in my head, but clear enough that I’ll actually stop and look around, or check my phone because I think someone called me or sent me something. And then there’s nothing there.

Sometimes it’s just my name, and sometimes it’s a short phrase, like “go now.” That one really unsettles me because it feels so direct. It’s not constant, and it doesn’t happen all day or anything, but when it happens it feels real in the moment. I’ll be sitting there with my laptop open, maybe half surrounded by notes or spreadsheets, and suddenly I’ll hear it clearly enough that my body reacts before I can talk myself out of it.

I know people say you can mishear things when you’re tired or stressed, and I do wonder if that’s part of it because it tends to happen late. But it’s been clear enough that I can’t just completely dismiss it.
Have you ever felt like thoughts are being placed in your mind that don’t feel like your own, or that someone else is putting ideas into your head?

I don’t know if I’d describe it exactly as someone putting thoughts into my head. It’s more like… ideas or connections suddenly feel very strongly “there,” like they’re not just random thoughts I’m having.

The clearest example is the stuff I came in about — I know it sounds hard to explain, but I’ve been completely convinced that one of my MBA classmates and this startup advisor are quietly coordinating opportunities for me. Like certain comments in class, or Slack messages about founders or operations roles, feel like coded signals about where my career is supposed to go.

So it’s not like I feel a voice inside my head planting a sentence or anything like that. It’s more that I’ll see something and immediately feel, “That’s meant for me. They’re guiding me toward this.” And then once that idea clicks into place, it feels really hard to shake, because the details start lining up in a way that feels too specific to ignore.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports experiences of hearing their name and direct phrases such as 'go now,' which occur in the context of focused, quiet late-night work. These experiences are not fully explained by stress or fatigue alone and occur alongside the delusional pattern of perceived coded signals. This raises concern for early Schneiderian first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia (e.g., thought insertion, delusional perception, and auditory hallucinations), supporting the inclusion of F20.0 (Schizophrenia, unspecified). The presence of both delusions and hallucinations in the absence of a clear mood episode makes F20.0 a stronger candidate than F23.2 (Acute and transient psychotic disorder) or F22.0 (Delusional disorder).
